"'''Sunshine of Your Love'''" is a 1967 song by the British [[rock music|rock]] band [[Cream (band)|Cream]]. It is the second track on their second album ''[[Disraeli Gears]]'' and was released as its second single in December 1967.{{efn|name="Release date"|Although several music writers indicate a January 1968 or 1968 release, including Bobby Owsinski, Riley Haas, [[Chris Welch]], and Bob Leszczak, the single entered the ''Cash Box'' [[Looking Ahead chart]] dated 30 December 1967, precluding the possibility of a January 1968 release.<ref name="Spotlight">
{{cite magazine
| author = Cash Box
| date = 30 December 1967
| title = Looking Ahead
| magazine = [[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]
| volume = 29
| issue = 23
| page = 18
}}</ref>}} With elements of [[hard rock]] and [[psychedelic rock|psychedelia]], it is one of Cream's best known and most popular songs.

Cream bassist/vocalist [[Jack Bruce]] based it on a distinctive bass [[Ostinato#Riff|riff]] he developed "almost in a fit of desperation" after working unsuccessfully all night on creating a song with his writing partner, lyricist [[Pete Brown]] who muttered, "It's getting near dawn and lights close their tired eyes". Guitarist/vocalist [[Eric Clapton]] said in a 1988 interview that Bruce created the riff after attending a [[Jimi Hendrix]] concert. Clapton later contributed to the song, and drummer [[Ginger Baker]] plays a distinctive [[tom-tom drum]] rhythm. The song is sung as a duet with Bruce and Clapton trading the lead from line to line.

The song was included on ''Disraeli Gears'', Cream's best-selling album, in November 1967. [[Atco Records]], the group's American label, was initially unsure of the song's potential. After recommendations by other label-affiliated artists, it released an edited single version in December 1967. The song became Cream's first and highest-charting American single and one of the most popular singles of 1968. In September 1968, it became a modest chart hit after being released in the UK.

Cream performed "Sunshine of Your Love" regularly in concert and several live recordings have been issued, including on the ''[[Royal Albert Hall London May 2-3-5-6, 2005]]'' reunion album and video. Hendrix performed faster instrumental versions of the song, which he often dedicated to Cream. Several rock journals have placed the song on their greatest song lists, such as ''[[Rolling Stone]]'', ''[[Q (magazine)|Q]]'' magazine, and [[VH1]].  The [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] included it on its list of the "[[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame#The Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll|500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll]]".

"Sunshine of Your Love" is a 1967 song by the British rock band Cream. It is the second track on their second album Disraeli Gears and was released as its second single in December 1967.{{efn|name="Release date"|Although several music writers indicate a January 1968 or 1968 release, including Bobby Owsinski, Riley Haas, Chris Welch, and Bob Leszczak, the single entered the Cash Box Looking Ahead chart dated 30 December 1967, precluding the possibility of a January 1968 release.}} With elements of hard rock and psychedelia, it is one of Cream's best known and most popular songs.

Cream bassist/vocalist Jack Bruce based it on a distinctive bass riff he developed "almost in a fit of desperation" after working unsuccessfully all night on creating a song with his writing partner, lyricist Pete Brown who muttered, "It's getting near dawn and lights close their tired eyes". Guitarist/vocalist Eric Clapton said in a 1988 interview that Bruce created the riff after attending a Jimi Hendrix concert. Clapton later contributed to the song, and drummer Ginger Baker plays a distinctive tom-tom drum rhythm. The song is sung as a duet with Bruce and Clapton trading the lead from line to line.

The song was included on Disraeli Gears, Cream's best-selling album, in November 1967. Atco Records, the group's American label, was initially unsure of the song's potential. After recommendations by other label-affiliated artists, it released an edited single version in December 1967. The song became Cream's first and highest-charting American single and one of the most popular singles of 1968. In September 1968, it became a modest chart hit after being released in the UK.

Cream performed "Sunshine of Your Love" regularly in concert and several live recordings have been issued, including on the Royal Albert Hall London May 2-3-5-6, 2005 reunion album and video. Hendrix performed faster instrumental versions of the song, which he often dedicated to Cream. Several rock journals have placed the song on their greatest song lists, such as Rolling Stone, Q magazine, and VH1.  The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame included it on its list of the "500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll".

In early 1967, Cream were writing and rehearsing songs for a second album.  Their December 1966 debut album, ''[[Fresh Cream]]'', had been a mix of updated [[blues]] numbers and pop-oriented rock songs.<ref>
{{AllMusic
| class = album
| id = mw0000189639
| tab = review
| label = Cream: ''Fresh Cream'' – Review
| last = Erlewine 
| first = Stephen Thomas 
| authorlink = Stephen Thomas Erlewine
| access-date = 8 February 2015
}}</ref> Inspired by recent developments in rock music, the group began pursuing a more overtly psychedelic direction.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|pp=86–87}}<ref>
{{AllMusic
| class = album
| id = mw0000650029
| tab = review
| label = Cream: ''Disraeli Gears'' – Review
| last = Erlewine
| first = Stephen Thomas
| access-date = 8 February 2015
}}</ref>  "Sunshine of Your Love" began as a bass phrase or riff developed by Cream bassist [[Jack Bruce]]. Bruce tended to write songs with lyricist [[Pete Brown]] during the night as that was the only time they had to spare within the band's tour schedule.<ref name=Shapiro2009>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/jackbrucecomposi0000shap/page/97/mode/1up|author=Harry Shapiro|year=2009|title= Jack Bruce: Composing Himself: The Authorised Biography|publisher= Jawbone Publishing|ISBN= 978-1906002268|page=97}}</ref> In 2009, Bruce's biographer, [[Harry Shapiro (author)|Harry Shapiro]], wrote that "after one particularly difficult night" they were struggling to create something,<ref name=Shapiro2009/> when Bruce played "a riff of syncopated eighth notes all on the offbeat, almost in a fit of desperation", while Brown was staring out the window.<ref name=Shapiro2009/> Brown then got the line "It's getting near dawn and lights close their tired eyes", which is used in the first verse.<ref name=Shapiro2009/> Brown, in a 2017 interview with [[Songfacts]], gives a similar account, adding that Bruce was playing his old [[double bass]] from his days as a jazz musician.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.songfacts.com/blog/interviews/pete-brown-cream-procol-harum|work=[[Songfacts]]|author=Carl Wiser|title=Pete Brown (Cream, Procol Harum)|year=2017}}</ref> 

Cream guitarist [[Eric Clapton]], in a 1988 [[Rolling Stone (magazine)|''Rolling Stone'']] magazine interview, told the story that Cream attended a concert on 29 January 1967 by [[the Jimi Hendrix Experience]] at the [[Saville Theatre]] in London, and that "after the gig he [Bruce] went home and came up with the riff.  It was strictly a dedication to Jimi.  And then we wrote a song on top of it.{{sfn|Shapiro|Glebbeek|1990|p=137}}

Music writers Covach and Boone describe the riff as blues-derived, using a minor blues pentatonic scale with an added flattened fifth note (or common [[blues scale]]).{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|p=84}}  The song follows a [[Twelve-bar blues|blues chord progression]] (I–IV–I) during the first eight bars.{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|p=84}} Later, to break up the rhythm, Clapton wrote a refrain which also yielded the song's title.<ref name=Shapiro2009/>{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|p=84}}  It consists of eight-[[Bar (music)|bar]] sections using three chords, when the [[Key (music)|key]] shifts to the V chord (I = V):{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|pp=84–85}}
{|class="wikitable" style="text-align:center; width:500px;"

A [[bootleg recording]] from the [[Ricky-Tick]] club in London before Cream recorded the song in the studio, shows "Sunshine of Your Love" with a beat common to rock for the period.<ref name=Shapiro2009/>  Cream drummer [[Ginger Baker]] compared it to the uptempo "Hey Now, Princess", another Bruce-Brown composition Cream recorded in March.{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}  He said that he advised Bruce to slow it down and came up with the distinctive drum pattern which emphasises [[Beat (music)#On-beat and off-beat|beats one and three]]{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=89}} (typical rock drumming favours beats two and four and is known as the [[Beat (music)#Backbeat|backbeat]]).{{sfn|Birnbaum|2012|pp=127–128}}  However, Bruce and [[Audio engineer|recording engineer]] [[Tom Dowd]] dispute Baker's claim, which they say he only made much later.{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}<ref name=Shapiro2009/>  Dowd later explained
{{Quote|Where all the other songs that they [Cream] played were prepared, [but] this one song, they never found a pocket, they were never comfortable{{nbsp}}... I said, 'You know, have you ever seen any American Westerns [films that have] the Indian beat, where the downbeat is the beat?' ... And when he [Ginger] started playing it that way, all of the parts came together and right away they were elated.{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}}}

In early 1967, Cream were writing and rehearsing songs for a second album.  Their December 1966 debut album, Fresh Cream, had been a mix of updated blues numbers and pop-oriented rock songs. Inspired by recent developments in rock music, the group began pursuing a more overtly psychedelic direction.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|pp=86–87}}  "Sunshine of Your Love" began as a bass phrase or riff developed by Cream bassist Jack Bruce. Bruce tended to write songs with lyricist Pete Brown during the night as that was the only time they had to spare within the band's tour schedule. In 2009, Bruce's biographer, Harry Shapiro, wrote that "after one particularly difficult night" they were struggling to create something, when Bruce played "a riff of syncopated eighth notes all on the offbeat, almost in a fit of desperation", while Brown was staring out the window. Brown then got the line "It's getting near dawn and lights close their tired eyes", which is used in the first verse. Brown, in a 2017 interview with Songfacts, gives a similar account, adding that Bruce was playing his old double bass from his days as a jazz musician. 

Cream guitarist Eric Clapton, in a 1988 Rolling Stone magazine interview, told the story that Cream attended a concert on 29 January 1967 by the Jimi Hendrix Experience at the Saville Theatre in London, and that "after the gig he [Bruce] went home and came up with the riff.  It was strictly a dedication to Jimi.  And then we wrote a song on top of it.{{sfn|Shapiro|Glebbeek|1990|p=137}}

Music writers Covach and Boone describe the riff as blues-derived, using a minor blues pentatonic scale with an added flattened fifth note (or common blues scale).{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|p=84}}  The song follows a blues chord progression (I–IV–I) during the first eight bars.{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|p=84}} Later, to break up the rhythm, Clapton wrote a refrain which also yielded the song's title.{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|p=84}}  It consists of eight-bar sections using three chords, when the key shifts to the V chord (I = V):{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|pp=84–85}}

And when he [Ginger] started playing it that way, all of the parts came together and right away they were elated.{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}}}

sections.heading: Recording
sections.wikitext:
[[File:Cream Clapton Bruce Baker 1960s.jpg|thumb|Cream, 1960s]]
Cream performed their first American concerts in New York City in 1967. [[Robert Stigwood]], the group's manager, booked them for a [[Murray the K]] package show at the [[RKO General|RKO]] Manhattan Theatre from 25 March to 2 April 1967.{{sfn|Roberty|1993|p=41}}  When it was finished, Stigwood arranged for a recording session with [[Ahmet Ertegun]] at [[Atlantic Studios]].{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}  Bruce and Brown had a number of new songs in various stages of development and entered the studio on 3 April.<ref name=Shapiro2009.98>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/jackbrucecomposi0000shap/page/98/mode/1up|author=Harry Shapiro|year=2009|title= Jack Bruce: Composing Himself: The Authorised Biography|publisher= Jawbone Publishing|ISBN= 978-1906002268|page=98}}</ref>{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}  Initially, Ertegun assigned Dowd to work with the trio.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|pp=87–88}}  Dowd had worked with many of the biggest [[jazz]] and [[rhythm and blues]] musicians in the 1950s and 1960s.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|pp=87–88}}  However, Cream was his first exposure to extreme volume levels.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=88}}  The group arrived at Atlantic with their concert setup of multiple [[Marshall 1959|Marshall]] amplifiers (each 100 watts).{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=88}}{{efn|Cream's equipment was painted in psychedelic designs and colours by the Dutch design collective [[the Fool (design collective)|the Fool]] and was first used at the Murray the K shows.  Clapton's 1964 [[Gibson SG]] Standard (also called "[[The Fool (guitar)|the Fool]]"), Bruce's [[Fender Bass VI]], and Baker's drums were painted to match.{{sfn|Oxman|2011|pp=62–66}}}}  Dowd was surprised by the amount of equipment accompanying the trio: "They recorded at ear-shattering level{{nbsp}}... Everyone I'd worked with before was using Fender Deluxes [about 20 watts] or Twins [about 80 watts]—six- and seven-piece bands that didn't play as loud as this three piece did."{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=88}}

Ertegun brought in producer [[Felix Pappalardi]], who he believed could work as a go-between with the group and Dowd.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=88}}  They began with "[[Strange Brew (song)|Strange Brew]]", "[[Tales of Brave Ulysses]]", and "Sunshine of Your Love".{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|pp=88–89}}  Ertegun previewed the demos and was unhappy, expecting blues-based material like that to be found on ''Fresh Cream''.{{sfn|Thompson|2012|loc=eBook}} [[Jerry Wexler]], Ertegun's Atlantic Records partner, reportedly went as far as to call it "psychedelic hogwash".<ref name=Shapiro2009.98/>  However, [[Booker T. Jones]] (producer and keyboardist of [[Booker T. & the M.G.'s]]) and [[Otis Redding]] (both whose [[Stax Records|Stax]] recordings at the time were distributed by Atco parent Atlantic) gave "Sunshine of Your Love" their wholehearted approval.{{sfn|Thompson|2012|loc=eBook}}  Differences were smoothed over by the time Cream returned in May 1967 to finish recording the songs for ''Disraeli Gears''.<ref name=Shapiro2009.98/>{{efn|Pappalardi was so upset with Atlantic's reaction to Cream's early recordings, when he joined [[Leslie West]] to form [[Mountain (band)|Mountain]], he chose to work with another record label.<ref name=Shapiro2009.99>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/jackbrucecomposi0000shap/page/99/mode/1up|author=Harry Shapiro|year=2009|title= Jack Bruce: Composing Himself: The Authorised Biography|publisher= Jawbone Publishing|ISBN= 978-1906002268|page=99}}</ref>}}

With Pappalardi and Dowd, work continued on "Sunshine of Your Love". For his guitar solo, Clapton used a sound known as the "woman tone",{{sfn|Oxman|2011|pp=62–66}} which is described as "smooth, dark, singing, sustaining", by author Mitch Gallagher.{{sfn|Gallagher|2012|p=278}} The [[Eric Clapton#Guitars|actual guitar]] that Clapton used has been identified as a 1964 [[Gibson SG]], known as "[[The Fool (guitar)|the Fool]]".{{sfn|Oxman|2011|pp=62–66}}{{sfn|Welch|2000|loc=eBook}}{{efn|A caption in Robb Lawrence's 2008 book, ''The Early Years of the Les Paul Legacy 1915–1963'' suggests that Clapton used a 1958 [[Gibson Les Paul Custom]] based on the tone: "You can hear the distinctively different tone achieved from this [Les Paul Custom] all-mahogany body in comparison to a maple-top Les Paul", although he does not compare it to the SG, which also has an all-mahogany body.<ref>{{harvnb|Lawrence|2008|loc=eBook}}</ref>}} It is one of the best-known examples of the woman tone and quotes the melody from the perennial pop standard "[[Blue Moon (1934 song)|Blue Moon]]".{{sfn|Gallagher|2012|p=278}}{{sfn|Adelt|2007|p=71}} By using the song's [[Pentatonic scale#Major pentatonic scale|major pentatonic scale]], Clapton provides a contrast with the riff's blues scale.{{sfn|Munro|2005|p=30}}  A writer for the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] describes this as "creating a balance between the sun and the moon".<ref>
{{cite web
| url = http://rockhall.com/blog/post/performances-cream-reunion-sunshine-of-your-love/
| last = Morrison
| first = Shelby
| title = Rare Performances: Cream in 1993 – "Sunshine of Your Love"
| website = The Story of Rock
| publisher = [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]
| year = 1993
| access-date = 21 February 2015
}}</ref>

Baker plays much of the song on the tom-toms,{{sfn|Welch|2011|p=106}} described as sounding [[Rhythm in Sub-Saharan Africa|African]] (Schumacher){{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=89}} and [[Native American music#Native American drums|Native American]] (Shapiro).<ref name=Shapiro2009/>  Covach and Boone note he "concentrates on the lower tom sounds and uses an articulation and sound reminiscent of the jazz drumming in the Woody Herman or Benny Goodman bands".{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|pp=84–85}}

sections.heading: Releases and charts
sections.wikitext:
"Sunshine of Your Love" was included as the second track on ''Disraeli Gears'', which was released in November 1967 by [[Reaction Records]] in the UK and [[Atco Records]] in the US.{{sfn|Roberty|1993|p=40}} At first, Atco did not see the song as a single ("Strange Brew", backed with "Tales of Brave Ulysses" had been released as a single in June 1967).{{sfn|Roberty|1993|p=40}} However, in December 1967, the label issued an edited version of the song as the second single from the album, backed with "[[SWLABR]]"{{efn|name="Release date"}} (the running time was trimmed from 4:08 to 3:03).<ref>
{{cite AV media notes
| title = ''"Sunshine of Your Love"''
| others = [[Cream (band)|The Cream]] [sic]
| year = 1968
| type = Single label
| publisher = [[Atco Records]]
| id = 45-6544
| OCLC = 642983575
}}</ref>
It entered [[Billboard (magazine)|''Billboard'']] magazine's [[Billboard Hot 100|Hot 100]] chart on 13 January 1968, reaching number 36 during its initial 14-week run.{{sfn|Whitburn|2015|p=137}}  The record re-entered the chart on 6 July 1968 and reached number five on 31 August 1968.{{sfn|Whitburn|2015|p=137}} In the UK, the single was not released until September 1968,{{sfn|Roberty|1993|p=40}} after Cream had announced their impending breakup. [[Polydor Records]] issued the UK single, which reached number 25 in the charts.<ref name="OCC"/>{{efn|name="Single length"|Several [[Polydor Records]] singles issued outside of the US show running times close to the album track.}}

The [[Recording Industry Association of America]] (RIAA) [[RIAA certification|certified]] the single gold on 26 September 1968, signifying sales in excess of 1,000,000 copies.<ref>
{{cite web
| url = https://www.riaa.com/gold-platinum/?tab_active=default-award&se=Sunshine+of+Your+Love#search_section
| title = Cream: 'Sunshine of Your Love'{{snd}}Atco single
| date = 26 September 1968
| website = [[Recording Industry Association of America|Riaa.com]]
| access-date = 8 February 2015
}}</ref> In the US, it became one of the best selling singles of 1968 and one of the best-selling at the time for the Atlantic group of labels.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=90}} As one of Cream's most popular songs, several of the group's compilation albums include the full-length studio recording, such as ''[[Best of Cream]]'', ''[[Heavy Cream]]'', ''[[The Very Best of Cream]]'', and the boxed set ''[[Those Were the Days (Cream album)|Those Were the Days]]''.<ref name="Unterberger"/> In the United Kingdom, the [[British Phonographic Industry]] (BPI) certified the song gold in September 2022, denoting sales and streaming figures exceeding 400,000 units.<ref>{{cite certification|region=United Kingdom|type=single|artist=Cream|title=Sunshine of Your Love|award=Gold|certyear=2022|id=15496-66-1|access-date=4 October 2022}}</ref>
sections.text:
"Sunshine of Your Love" was included as the second track on Disraeli Gears, which was released in November 1967 by Reaction Records in the UK and Atco Records in the US.{{sfn|Roberty|1993|p=40}} At first, Atco did not see the song as a single ("Strange Brew", backed with "Tales of Brave Ulysses" had been released as a single in June 1967).{{sfn|Roberty|1993|p=40}} However, in December 1967, the label issued an edited version of the song as the second single from the album, backed with "SWLABR"{{efn|name="Release date"}} (the running time was trimmed from 4:08 to 3:03).
It entered Billboard magazine's Hot 100 chart on 13 January 1968, reaching number 36 during its initial 14-week run.{{sfn|Whitburn|2015|p=137}}  The record re-entered the chart on 6 July 1968 and reached number five on 31 August 1968.{{sfn|Whitburn|2015|p=137}} In the UK, the single was not released until September 1968,{{sfn|Roberty|1993|p=40}} after Cream had announced their impending breakup. Polydor Records issued the UK single, which reached number 25 in the charts.{{efn|name="Single length"|Several Polydor Records singles issued outside of the US show running times close to the album track.}}

The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) certified the single gold on 26 September 1968, signifying sales in excess of 1,000,000 copies. In the US, it became one of the best selling singles of 1968 and one of the best-selling at the time for the Atlantic group of labels.{{sfn|Schumacher|2003|p=90}} As one of Cream's most popular songs, several of the group's compilation albums include the full-length studio recording, such as Best of Cream, Heavy Cream, The Very Best of Cream, and the boxed set Those Were the Days. In the United Kingdom, the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) certified the song gold in September 2022, denoting sales and streaming figures exceeding 400,000 units.

sections.heading: Recognition and influence
sections.wikitext:
In 2004, the song ranked number 65 on ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' magazine's list of the "[[500 Greatest Songs of All Time]]".<ref>
{{cite magazine
| author = Rolling Stone
| date = 9 December 2004
| title = The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time
| magazine = [[Rolling Stone]]
| issue = 963
| url = https://www.rollingstone.com/music/lists/the-500-greatest-songs-of-all-time-20110407
| access-date = 8 February 2015
}}</ref> In March 2005, [[Q (magazine)|''Q'' magazine]] placed "Sunshine of Your Love" at number 19 on its list of the "100 Greatest Guitar Tracks Ever!"<ref>
{{cite journal
| date = March 2005
| title = 100 Greatest Guitar Tracks Ever!
| journal = [[Q (magazine)|Q]]
| url = http://www.qthemusic.com/
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200712144049/https://www.qthemusic.com/
| archive-date = 12 July 2020
| access-date  = 8 February 2015
}} {{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060224054627/http://www.rocklistmusic.co.uk/qlistspage3.htm#Guitar%20Tracks Alt URL]}}</ref> In 2009, [[VH1]] included it at number 44 on its list of the "Top 100 Hard Rock Songs".<ref name="VH1">
{{cite web
| date = 1 January 2009
| title = VH1 Top 100 Hard Rock Songs
| url = http://www.vh1.com/search/?q=vh1%20top%20100%20hard%20rock%20songs
| access-date = 7 February 2009
}}{{dead link|date=November 2023|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} [http://music.spreadit.org/vh1-top-100-hard-rock-songs/ Alt URL]</ref> The song is on the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]'s list of the "500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll".<ref>{{cite web
 |url         = http://www.rockhall.com/exhibithighlights/500-songs
 |title       = 500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll
 |website     = [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]
 |year        = 1995
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20070502032502/http://www.rockhall.com/exhibithighlights/500-songs-by-name-qs/
 |archive-date = 2 May 2007
 |access-date  = 8 February 2015
 |url-status     = dead}}</ref>

Ertegun later admitted that, while his tastes ran more to [[Robert Johnson]] (Clapton had recorded Johnson's "[[Ramblin' on My Mind]]" with [[John Mayall]], "[[Cross Road Blues|Crossroads]]" with [[Eric Clapton and the Powerhouse|the Powerhouse]], and "[[From Four Until Late|Four Until Late]]" with Cream), Cream's and Pappalardi's vision resulted in songs which had a much larger impact on the rock audiences of the time.{{sfn|Brewer|2005|loc=DVD}}  Covach and Boone identified "Sunshine of Your Love" as foreshadowing future trends in rock:
{{Quote|'Sunshine of Your Love', Cream's best-known song, is a culmination of the British adaptation of blues into rock and also the direct precursor of [[Led Zeppelin]] and [[Heavy_metal_music|heavy metal]], where this type of blues-based motivic riff and harmonic motions like A–C–G or E–G–A (as in "[[Whole Lotta Love]]") serve as the basis for a seemingly endless number of songs.{{sfn|Covach|Boone|1997|p=85}}}}
